ortho.priesthood_authority:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that the authority of the priesthood comes from Christ through the bishops, who stand in apostolic succession. A priest is ordained by a bishop and acts with the bishop's blessing. Without that authorization, he cannot celebrate the sacraments.

This is expressed in practice by the antimension, a cloth signed by the bishop and placed on the altar, which authorizes the celebration of the Divine Liturgy in a church. The authority is understood as service to the church, and not as a personal possession or rank. A Protestant reader whose tradition understands ministerial authority as coming from a local congregation or a denomination should note that the Orthodox tradition traces it to the continuous ministry of the bishops, going back to the apostles.
baptist.priesthood_of_believers:
Baptists hold to the priesthood of believers, which they often express in the phrase soul competency: every person is able to come to God directly, through Christ, without a priest or other human mediator, and is responsible before God for his own faith. Each believer may read and interpret Scripture, pray and serve God.

This is a key reason for Baptist convictions about religious freedom, the autonomy of the local church and baptism upon profession of faith. It does not mean that Baptists reject pastors or teachers, but that they understand these as servants of the congregation, and not as a higher class of Christian. A Protestant reader will find the idea familiar from Luther's teaching of the priesthood of all believers, and should note that Baptists have made it a central principle of church life.
catholic.priesthood_of_believers:
Catholics teach a common priesthood of the faithful: all the baptized share in Christ's priesthood, and are called to offer their lives, prayers and work to God as spiritual sacrifices, and to bear witness to Christ in the world. This is affirmed by the Second Vatican Council.

The Church holds that this common priesthood exists alongside the ministerial priesthood of the ordained, and does not replace it. The two are ordered to each other, so that the ordained serve the whole body. A Protestant reader who knows the priesthood of all believers as a principle that removes the need for a separate class of priests should note that Catholics hold both, and believe that Christ instituted the ordained priesthood to serve the priestly people.
lds.priesthood_of_believers:
The idea that all believers are priests is understood by Latter-day Saints in a different way. They speak of the general priesthood, meaning the Aaronic and Melchizedek priesthoods held by male members of the church, in offices such as deacon, elder and high priest, and used in a lay ministry, without professional clergy.

The Book of Mormon and the Bible also speak of all people becoming kings and priests, meaning those who make sacred covenants, and women are understood to take part in priesthood ordinances and to act with delegated authority in their callings, though not ordained to offices. A Protestant reader familiar with the priesthood of all believers should note that Latter-day Saints use similar language, but in a system where the priesthood is an ordained authority held by men.
lds.prophetic_authority:
Latter-day Saints sustain the president of the church as prophet, seer and revelator, and believe that he receives revelation from God for the church as a whole. The counselors in the First Presidency and the members of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles are also sustained as prophets, seers and revelators.

Members raise their hands to sustain their leaders in solemn assemblies, and they listen to their teachings at general conference. The church does not teach that the president is infallible, and acknowledges that leaders are human, and members are encouraged to seek their own confirmation through prayer. The authority of a prophet is understood to guide the church, not to replace the individual conscience. A Protestant reader who holds that revelation is complete in Scripture should note that the living prophet is central to Latter-day Saint identity.
new_apostolic.prophetic_authority:
In the New Apostolic Church, the Chief Apostle is the head of the apostle ministry worldwide. Members understand this office as the ministry through which Christ preserves the unity of the church, and the other apostles as the Chief Apostle's co-workers who serve in various regions.

The Chief Apostle is not regarded as sinless or as a source of new Scripture. He is understood as the one entrusted with guiding the church's teaching and care, and members honor him as Christ's representative in that task. Church life is organized around this shared apostolic ministry, and members pray for the Chief Apostle regularly. A Protestant reader from a church without such an office should note that it is understood in terms of unity and service, and does not claim to add to the Bible.
pentecostal.prophetic_authority:
Some Pentecostal and charismatic groups recognize prophets as a ministry office, referring to the list of ministries given to the church in the Letter to the Ephesians. Such a person is understood to have a recurring gift of prophecy and to serve the church by speaking what the Spirit gives.

Views and practice differ considerably. Many classical Pentecostal denominations speak mainly of the gift of prophecy exercised by any believer, and do not give a formal office of prophet special authority. Where prophets are recognized, their words are to be tested against Scripture and judged by the local church. A Protestant reader should note that no Pentecostal body holds that a prophet's words carry authority equal to the Bible, and pastors and elders remain responsible for the oversight of the church.
seventh_day_adventist.prophetic_authorit:
Seventh-day Adventists believe that the gift of prophecy was manifested in the ministry of Ellen G. White, a leader in the early Adventist movement in the nineteenth century, and they call her writings the Spirit of Prophecy. They regard her as a messenger of God who provided guidance, encouragement and correction to the church.

Her writings are treated as authoritative counsel, but they are not the basis of doctrine, which rests on Scripture alone. The church teaches that her writings must be tested by the Bible, and that they are not a substitute for it. A Protestant reader who holds that Scripture is the only authority should note that Adventists agree that Scripture is the final standard, and treat her ministry as a subordinate gift that helps the church to apply it.
anglican.purgatory:
The Thirty-Nine Articles reject the Roman doctrine of purgatory, as it was taught at the time of the Reformation, as having no warrant in Scripture. Anglicans speak instead of the intermediate state, the condition of the faithful departed between death and the resurrection, held in the care of God.

Modern Anglicans differ. Many simply commit the departed to God's mercy and speak of rest and growth in his presence. Some, especially Anglo-Catholics, pray for the dead and are open to the idea of cleansing or growth after death without adopting every part of the Catholic teaching. Others avoid prayers for the dead altogether. A Protestant reader who rejects purgatory should note that the Anglican formularies agree, while modern Anglican practice is less uniform, and includes a wider range of views.
catholic.purgatory:
Catholics teach that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but are not yet fully purified, undergo a purification after death, called purgatory, so that they can attain the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven. It is not a second chance, since those in purgatory are already saved, and it is not a permanent state.

The Church bases this teaching on the tradition of praying for the dead, on the passage in the second book of Maccabees, and on the image of a person saved as through fire in the First Letter to the Corinthians. Catholics can help those in purgatory by their prayers, by Masses and by works of charity. The Church has not defined its details, such as its duration. A Protestant reader who believes that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for all sin should note that Catholics see purgatory as the completion of God's work of making the saved holy.
ortho.purgatory:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not teach the Catholic doctrine of purgatory. It does not hold that the dead must satisfy a temporal punishment for sin, or that there is a distinct place of purification. It teaches that after death the soul experiences a particular judgment, and that the state of the dead before the Last Judgment is one in which the prayers of the living may help.

There is a tradition of the soul's passage after death, sometimes called the toll houses, in which the soul is tested by spirits, which some Orthodox accept as a spiritual teaching and others reject as unfounded. The church has not defined it. The Orthodox emphasize God's mercy and the church's prayer for the departed. A Protestant reader who rejects purgatory should note that the Orthodox reject the Western doctrine, but still pray for the dead.
adventist.rapture:
Adventists reject the teaching of a secret rapture, in which believers are taken from the earth before a period of tribulation. They teach that Christ's return will be visible, audible and glorious, seen by all the world, as described in the Gospel of Matthew, and that it will be a single event.

At that coming, they teach, the righteous dead will be raised, and the righteous living will be changed and taken to be with Christ, while the wicked will be destroyed by the brightness of his coming. They see the idea of a secret coming before the real one as unsupported by Scripture. A Protestant reader from an Evangelical tradition that teaches a pretribulation rapture should note that Adventists read the same passages, including those in the First Letter to the Thessalonians, as describing the one open Second Coming.
catholic.rapture:
The Catholic Church does not teach a rapture in the sense of a secret event that would take believers out of the world before a time of tribulation. That idea developed among some Protestants in the nineteenth century, and is not part of Catholic tradition.

Catholics do believe in the Second Coming of Christ, when he will come in glory to judge the living and the dead. They read the passage in the First Letter to the Thessalonians, about the dead in Christ rising and the living being caught up to meet the Lord, as part of that single event, the general resurrection and the Last Judgment. The Church leaves the details of the end times open and urges believers to be ready. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics do not attach the word rapture to a separate event.
evangelical.rapture:
Many Evangelicals believe in the rapture: the event in which believers will be caught up to meet Christ in the air, as described in the First Letter to the Thessalonians. It is most commonly associated with dispensational premillennialism, and has been widely popularized through study Bibles and novels.

Evangelicals differ about the timing. Some teach that it takes place before a period of great tribulation, called the pretribulation rapture, others that it is in the middle or after it. Many Evangelicals, especially in Reformed and other traditions, do not teach a rapture separate from the Second Coming of Christ at all. What all share is the hope that Christ will return and that believers will be with him forever. A Protestant reader should note that the rapture is a popular teaching among Evangelicals but is not held by all Protestants.
baptist.real_presence:
Baptists generally understand the Lord's Supper as an ordinance of remembrance. The bread and the juice or wine are symbols of Christ's body and blood, and the meal is a memorial of his death and a way of proclaiming it until he returns. They do not teach that the elements change or that Christ is present in them.

Baptists do say that Christ is present with his people when they gather and, by faith, in the observance of the ordinance. Many Baptist churches use unfermented grape juice, and hold the Supper monthly or quarterly. A Protestant reader from a Lutheran, Anglican or Reformed church, which teaches a more substantial presence of Christ in the Supper, should note that Baptists emphasize the meal as an act of obedience and remembrance, and stress that its meaning lies in faith and not in the elements.
catholic.real_presence:
Catholics teach the Real Presence: that after the priest says the words of consecration at Mass, the bread and wine become the body and blood, soul and divinity of Jesus Christ. The Church calls this change transubstantiation, meaning that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into that of Christ, while the appearances of bread and wine remain.

Catholics believe this on the strength of Jesus' words at the Last Supper, this is my body, and in the teaching of John chapter six. Because Christ is truly present, Catholics reserve the consecrated bread in tabernacles, and adore him, and hold processions such as the feast of Corpus Christi. A Protestant reader should note that Protestants hold a range of views, from the symbolic to the spiritual to the sacramental, and that Catholics teach a real presence of Christ himself in the elements.
lutheran.real_presence:
Lutherans teach the real presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper: the true body and blood of Christ are present in, with and under the bread and wine, and all who receive them receive Christ's body and blood, some to their blessing and some, if they do not believe, to their judgment. This is often called the sacramental union.

Lutherans hold this on the basis of Jesus' words, this is my body, this is my blood, taken as they stand. They do not teach that the bread and wine cease to be bread and wine, as in transubstantiation, and they do not treat the meal as a memorial only. A Protestant reader from a Reformed or Baptist church should note that Lutherans teach a bodily presence of Christ, which they receive in faith as a mystery, and trust his promise that the meal gives forgiveness of sins, life and salvation.
ortho.real_presence:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that in the Divine Liturgy the bread and wine, through the prayer of the priest and the descent of the Holy Spirit, become the true body and blood of Christ. This is sometimes called the change of the gifts. The Orthodox believe in the real presence, and receive communion in both kinds, with leavened bread.

They do not attempt to explain how the change happens, and they treat it as a holy mystery, so they are not comfortable with the philosophical terms used in the West, such as transubstantiation, though some Orthodox writers have used similar language. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox teaching is that the gifts truly become Christ's body and blood, and that it is not a memorial only, and that the moment of change is associated with the prayer for the Holy Spirit.
reformed.real_presence:
Reformed Christians, following John Calvin, teach that Christ is truly present in the Lord's Supper, but spiritually and not physically. The bread and wine remain bread and wine, and yet by the work of the Holy Spirit believers who receive them in faith are truly fed with Christ himself, and are united to him.

Calvin described it as the Spirit lifting believers up to heaven, where Christ is, to feed on him there. The Supper is therefore not a mere memorial, as some Christians teach, and not a change in the elements, as others teach. It is a sacrament in which God really gives what he promises. Views within the wider Reformed family have varied, and some individuals hold a more memorial view. A Protestant reader should note that the confessional Reformed teaching is a spiritual presence received by faith.
catholic.relics:
Catholics venerate relics, which are the bodily remains of saints, or objects that belonged to them or touched them. Relics are kept in churches, and every Catholic altar traditionally contains relics of saints. They are treated with reverence, and may be carried in processions or displayed for veneration.

The Church teaches that veneration is not worship, which belongs to God alone. Catholics honor relics because they honor the saints, whose bodies were temples of the Holy Spirit and will be raised, and because God has sometimes worked through such objects, as in the Old Testament account of a dead man revived by touching the bones of Elisha, and the account in Acts of cloths touched by Paul. A Protestant reader concerned about superstition should note that the Church teaches that relics have no power in themselves, and that any benefit is from God.
ortho.relics:
The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates holy relics, the bodies of saints, or parts of them, and objects associated with them. Relics are kept in churches, and the altar table contains relics of martyrs, and the antimension, the cloth on which the liturgy is celebrated, often has relics sewn into it.

The Orthodox teach that the bodies of the saints have been made holy by the Holy Spirit who dwelled in them, and that God works through them, as he did through the bones of Elisha in the Old Testament. Some saints' bodies are found incorrupt, or give off fragrant oil. Veneration is expressed by kissing the relics, and praying before them, and it is not worship. A Protestant reader who regards such practices as superstitious should note that the Orthodox see them as flowing from belief in the resurrection of the body and the sanctifying presence of the Spirit.
catholic.repentance:
Catholics understand repentance as conversion of heart: sorrow for sin because it offends God, and a resolve to change. The Church calls the interior act contrition. Perfect contrition arises from love of God, and imperfect contrition arises from fear of punishment or from the ugliness of sin. Both are used by God.

The sacrament of Reconciliation is the ordinary way in which grave sin is forgiven after Baptism. Repentance is not a single emotional crisis, but a habit of returning to God, which is expressed in Lent, in days of penance and in the confession of sins. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and Protestants agree that repentance is a turning from sin to God, and should note that Catholics give it a sacramental form, in which absolution is received from a priest.
lds.repentance:
Latter-day Saints teach that repentance is a change of heart and life, made possible by the Atonement of Jesus Christ. It is the second principle of the gospel, after faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. The steps of repentance usually include recognizing sin, feeling sorrow, confessing to God, forsaking the sin, making restitution where possible, and forgiving others.

Serious sins are also confessed to a bishop, who helps the person to repent, and who may set restrictions on church participation for a time. Repentance is understood as a continuing process throughout life, and its fruit is forgiveness and peace. A Protestant reader will find the emphasis on faith and repentance familiar, and should note that Latter-day Saints stress forsaking sin and making amends, and treat confession to a church leader as part of the process for serious matters.
oneness_pentecostal.repentance:
Repentance is the first step in the Oneness Pentecostal understanding of how a person receives salvation. It means a real turning from sin toward God, with sorrow for wrongdoing and a decision to change one's life. It is not a matter of feeling regret only, but of a change of direction.

Following the apostle Peter's words in Acts, repentance leads to baptism in Jesus' name and to the receiving of the Holy Ghost. Members believe that repentance continues throughout the Christian life as the believer turns from sin again and again in obedience to God. A Protestant reader will find that Oneness Pentecostals agree that repentance is a turning to God, and should note that they regard it as the first part of a three-part new birth which includes baptism and the Holy Ghost.
ortho.repentance:
The Eastern Orthodox Church uses the Greek word metanoia for repentance, which means a change of mind, a turning of the whole person toward God. It is understood not only as sorrow for wrong actions but as a continuing reorientation of life, which is expected to last as long as life does.

Repentance is expressed in confession, fasting, prayer, prostrations and acts of mercy. The season of Great Lent is a time of special repentance. The Jesus Prayer, asking for mercy, is a regular means of it. The Orthodox emphasize healing more than guilt, and see repentance as the way to be freed from the passions. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox agree that repentance is a turning to God, and see it as a lifelong path more than a single event.
adventist.restoration:
Adventists see themselves as part of the remnant, a word drawn from the book of Revelation for those who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus. They understand their movement as called to proclaim the everlasting gospel to the world, as in the three angels' messages in Revelation, and to restore Bible truths that they believe had been neglected, such as the seventh-day Sabbath, the state of the dead and the health message.

This does not mean that Adventists believe that only they are saved. They teach that God has faithful people in all churches, and they understand the remnant as a call to a mission and not as a boast. A Protestant reader who knows the Reformation idea of returning to Scripture should note that Adventists see themselves as continuing that work, and that their sense of being a remnant carries a duty to share the message.
churches_of_christ.restoration:
Churches of Christ trace their heritage to the Restoration Movement, or Stone-Campbell Movement, which arose in the early nineteenth century in the United States. Its aim was to restore the church to the pattern of the New Testament, and by doing so to overcome the divisions of Christianity.

Members set aside human creeds and denominational names, and try to rely on the Bible alone for their teaching and practice, asking what the earliest churches believed and did. They hope this can lead to Christian unity based on Scripture. They recognize that the movement itself divided into several branches. A Protestant reader who values the Reformation return to Scripture should note that Churches of Christ carry the same conviction further, seeking to restore the whole pattern of New Testament worship and organization, and not only its doctrine.
lds.restoration:
Latter-day Saints speak of the Restoration: their belief that Jesus Christ's church, with its authority, teachings and ordinances, was lost after the time of the apostles, and was restored through Joseph Smith. They date it from 1820, when he had a vision of God the Father and Jesus Christ, and it continued with visits of angels, the translation of the Book of Mormon and the organization of the church in 1830.

The Restoration includes the priesthood authority, additional scripture, temples and living prophets and apostles. Latter-day Saints see it as a continuing process, with revelation still being given. A Protestant reader who thinks of the Reformation as the recovery of the gospel should note that Latter-day Saints honor the Reformers, but believe that the Reformation was a preparation, and that the full restoration of the church required new revelation and divine authority.
restorationist.restoration:
Restorationists share the aim of restoring the church to its New Testament pattern, in teaching, worship, names and organization. Their method is to set aside later traditions and human creeds and to go back to the Bible, asking what the first Christians believed and did.

Different Restorationist movements have carried this out in different ways. Some emphasize a return to New Testament practice through careful study, others emphasize that God himself has restored lost authority, teachings or offices. The result is a family of quite different churches, all sharing the conviction that Christian unity and faithfulness require going back to the source. A Protestant reader who knows the Reformation call to return to Scripture should note that Restorationists apply it more thoroughly, to the forms of the church as well as its doctrines.
catholic.resurrection_of_christ:
Catholics confess that Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead on the third day, as the Gospels tell, and that his risen body was real and glorified. The empty tomb and the appearances to the apostles and others are treated as historical events, and the Resurrection is the foundation of the Christian faith.

The Church celebrates it at Easter, which is preceded by the Triduum, the three days of Holy Thursday, Good Friday and the Easter Vigil. Catholics also celebrate the Resurrection every Sunday. They understand the Resurrection as the victory over sin and death, and the promise of the resurrection of the faithful, and they encounter the risen Lord in the Eucharist. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and Protestants agree on the central fact of Christ's bodily resurrection.
lds.resurrection_of_christ:
Latter-day Saints affirm that Jesus Christ rose from the dead in a physical, glorified body of flesh and bone, on the third day after his crucifixion. They accept the accounts in the Gospels, and also hold that the Book of Mormon records his appearance to people in the Americas after his resurrection.

They see his resurrection as the firstfruits of the resurrection of all people, and as the great sign that death is conquered. They celebrate Easter, and consider the Resurrection to be a central part of the Atonement, together with Gethsemane and the cross. A Protestant reader will find that Latter-day Saints share the belief in Christ's bodily resurrection, and should note the added belief that he appeared in the Americas, recorded in their scripture.
ortho.resurrection_of_christ:
The Eastern Orthodox Church celebrates the Resurrection of Christ at Pascha, the Orthodox name for Easter, which it calls the feast of feasts. The midnight service begins in darkness, and the light of a candle is passed among the people, and they greet one another with Christ is risen, and the reply, Truly he is risen.

The Orthodox icon of the Resurrection shows Christ descending to the realm of the dead and raising Adam and Eve from their tombs, which expresses their belief that Christ's death and resurrection destroyed death and freed humanity. A hymn sung at Pascha says that Christ trampled down death by death. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox share belief in the bodily resurrection, and should note that Orthodox worship makes the Resurrection the center of the whole year.
catholic.resurrection_of_the_dead:
Catholics confess the resurrection of the body: at the end of time, on the Last Day, all the dead will be raised, the just to eternal life and the wicked to eternal punishment. Their bodies will be raised and reunited with their souls, and the bodies of the saved will be transformed and glorified, as Christ's body was in his resurrection.

The Church teaches that the body is not a prison for the soul, but a good part of the human person, and that God will restore it. Between death and the resurrection, the souls of the saved are with Christ, and the faithful pray for those being purified. A Protestant reader will find this belief familiar, and should note that Catholics stress the unity of body and soul, and the continuity of the risen body with the earthly one.
jehovahs_witnesses.resurrection_of_the_d:
Jehovah's Witnesses look forward to a resurrection of the dead, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous, as taught in the book of Acts. Those who have been chosen for the heavenly calling are raised to spirit life in heaven, while the great majority are raised to life on earth in the coming new world.

They understand resurrection as an act of God's memory and power: Jehovah remembers those who have died, and recreates them with their identity and memories. Those raised will have the opportunity to learn about Jehovah and to serve him. A Protestant reader who expects the resurrection of the body at Christ's return should note that Witnesses connect the resurrection with their teaching that the dead are unconscious, and that most of the resurrected will live on a restored earth.
lds.resurrection_of_the_dead:
Latter-day Saints believe that because of Jesus Christ, every person who has lived will be resurrected: the spirit will be reunited with a physical body, which will be perfected, and will never die again. This is a free gift to all, whether righteous or wicked, and it does not depend on works.

They teach that the righteous will be resurrected first, at the time of Christ's Second Coming, in what is called the first resurrection, and the rest later, after the Millennium. The resurrected body is understood to be a body of flesh and bone, and Latter-day Saints stress its physical reality. A Protestant reader will find the belief in a universal bodily resurrection familiar, and should note that it is followed by a judgment that assigns people to different degrees of glory.
ortho.resurrection_of_the_dead:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that at Christ's second coming all the dead will be raised, and that the bodies of the saved will be transfigured, made incorruptible and glorious like Christ's risen body. The same body will be raised, but in a changed form, as the apostle Paul teaches in the First Letter to the Corinthians.

Pascha, the Orthodox Easter, is understood as a foretaste of the general resurrection, and the church speaks of the faithful departed as having fallen asleep in the Lord. The human being is understood as a unity of body and soul, and the body is honored, which is one reason why relics are venerated. A Protestant reader will find the hope of resurrection familiar, and should note that Orthodox worship keeps it constantly in view, in funeral hymns and in the celebration of the Resurrection each Sunday.
catholic.roman_catholic_label:
Catholics generally call themselves simply Catholic, and the Church calls itself the Catholic Church. The word catholic, meaning universal, is one of the marks of the Church in the Nicene Creed, and Catholics understand it as describing the Church that is present throughout the world.

The term Roman Catholic is also used, often in ecumenical, legal and popular contexts, to distinguish the Catholic Church from other Christian bodies, since many Protestants also say they are catholic in the sense of the Creed. Some Catholics do not like the addition of Roman, since it can suggest a local church, and since the Catholic Church includes Eastern churches whose rites are not Roman. A Protestant reader should note that either term is generally acceptable, and that Catholic is the preferred one, but Roman Catholic is widely understood and used.
ortho.roman_catholic_label:
Eastern Orthodox Christians commonly call the Catholic Church the Roman Catholic Church, and have historically called its members the Latins, referring to the Latin-speaking western church centered in Rome. They use these terms because they understand the word catholic in the Creed to describe the Orthodox Church, which they hold to have kept the fullness of the faith.

The name Roman is a way of identifying the Western church and its distinctive teaching, such as papal primacy, without granting that it alone is catholic. Some Orthodox use Catholic for the Roman church in a courteous way, and others avoid it. A Protestant reader should note that the labels carry the history of the division between East and West, and that each side sees itself as the Church of the Creed.
anglican.rosary:
Some Anglicans use Anglican prayer beads, a set of beads modeled loosely on the rosary but with a different structure, which are used for meditation, for the Jesus Prayer, for Psalms and for intercessory prayer. The beads help focus the mind and give a rhythm to prayer.

Some Anglo-Catholics also pray the traditional Rosary, with its prayers and meditations on the life of Christ and Mary. Use of either is a matter of personal devotion and is not required. Many Anglicans, particularly Evangelicals, do not use beads at all, and some are uneasy about devotion to Mary. A Protestant reader should note that where beads are used, they are understood as an aid to prayer and do not have power in themselves.
catholic.rosary:
The Rosary is a Catholic prayer, said with a string of beads, in which the person recites a series of prayers while meditating on events in the life of Jesus and Mary. It is made up of groups of ten Hail Marys, called decades, each introduced by an Our Father and closed with a short prayer of praise, called the Glory Be.

The meditations are called mysteries, and they are the joyful, sorrowful, glorious and luminous mysteries, covering the birth, ministry, death and resurrection of Christ. The Hail Mary is built from the angel Gabriel's greeting to Mary and Elizabeth's greeting to her, with a petition asking for her prayers. Catholics describe the Rosary as a Christ-centered prayer. A Protestant reader who is concerned about the repetition of words should note that Catholics say the repeated prayers as a background for meditation, as a way of keeping the mind on Christ.
ortho.rosary:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not use the Catholic Rosary, but has a comparable aid to prayer called the prayer rope, in Greek komboskini and in Russian chotki. It is a loop of knotted cord, usually with thirty-three, fifty or a hundred knots, and it is used to count repetitions of the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.

Monks use it a great deal, and many lay Orthodox Christians carry one, sometimes on the wrist. The knots are meant to keep the person's attention on prayer and are not a way of earning merit. A Protestant reader who is concerned about repeated prayers should note that the Orthodox teach that the Jesus Prayer should be prayed with attention, and that the rope is only an aid, like a bookmark, for maintaining focus.
adventist.sabbath:
Adventists keep the seventh-day Sabbath, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, as a day of rest and worship. They base this on the fourth of the Ten Commandments and on the account of creation in Genesis, in which God rested on the seventh day, and on the example of Jesus and the early church, who kept the Sabbath.

Adventists worship on Saturday, and spend the day in worship, study, family time and service, and refrain from ordinary work and business. They do not teach that keeping the Sabbath earns salvation, but regard it as a sign of loyalty to God the Creator and of trust in him. Most other Protestants worship on Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, and call it the Lord's Day, and some call it the Christian Sabbath. A Protestant reader should note that Adventists see the Sabbath as remaining on the seventh day and not transferred to Sunday.
catholic.sabbath:
Catholics observe Sunday as the Lord's Day, the day of Christ's resurrection, and they understand it as taking the place of the Sabbath of the Old Testament. The Church teaches that the commandment to keep the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that Sunday is the day when Christians gather for the Eucharist and rest from unnecessary work.

Catholics are obliged to attend Mass on Sundays and on holy days, and the Saturday evening Vigil Mass counts for this. They are also asked to refrain from work and business that prevent rest and worship, so far as possible. A Protestant reader from a church that keeps Sunday as the Christian Sabbath will find similarity, while Adventists and others who keep Saturday would note that Catholics regard the transfer to Sunday as rooted in the practice of the early church.
lds.sabbath:
Latter-day Saints keep Sunday as the Sabbath day, and regard it as holy time given by God for rest from daily labor, for worship and for renewing covenants. They attend church, take the sacrament, and spend the rest of the day with family, in study, prayer, service to others, and visiting the sick or lonely.

Members are encouraged to avoid shopping, sports, and other activities that distract from the purpose of the day, though how strictly this is applied varies. The observance is based on the commandment in Exodus and on statements in their own scriptures. A Protestant reader from a church that keeps Sunday as the Lord's Day will find the practice familiar, and should note that Latter-day Saints stress the sacrament and family life as central to the day.
messianic.sabbath:
Messianic believers commonly keep Shabbat, the seventh-day Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening. A typical observance includes lighting candles, a blessing over wine and bread, a family meal, rest from ordinary work, and congregational worship on Saturday with readings from the Torah and the Prophets.

Shabbat is treated as a joyful gift from God and as part of Jewish identity and practice which Jesus himself kept. Most Messianic believers do not teach that keeping it is required for salvation, and they generally do not judge other Christians who worship on Sunday. A Protestant reader from a church that observes Sunday as the Lord's Day should note that Messianic congregations usually meet on Saturday, and that observance varies from one congregation and family to another.
seventh_day_adventist.sabbath:
Seventh-day Adventists observe the Sabbath from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday. It is the seventh day of the week, which they hold to be the day God blessed and set apart at creation, and which the fourth of the Ten Commandments tells believers to remember. Their name comes from it.

The Sabbath begins with a welcome at home on Friday evening, and continues with Sabbath school and worship on Saturday, and often a shared meal and time in nature, and visits to those in need. Members refrain from ordinary work and commerce. Adventists teach that the Sabbath is a delight and a gift, and a sign of God as Creator and Redeemer. A Protestant reader who worships on Sunday should note that Adventists regard the Sabbath as a lasting commandment which has not been transferred to another day.
baptist.sacraments:
Baptists speak of two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper, and generally avoid the word sacraments. An ordinance is a rite which Christ commanded the church to observe. Baptists understand them as symbolic acts of obedience and remembrance, and as public professions of faith, and not as means by which grace is given.

Baptism, by immersion, pictures a believer's union with Christ in his death and resurrection, and the Lord's Supper proclaims his death. Baptists teach that the power of these acts lies in the faith of those who take part, and in Christ, and not in the water or the elements themselves. A Protestant reader from a Lutheran, Anglican or Reformed church, where the sacraments are means through which God gives grace, should note that Baptists deliberately use the word ordinance to say that the rites are signs and acts of obedience.
catholic.sacraments:
Catholics teach that there are seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Reconciliation, the Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony. A sacrament is defined as an outward sign, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, that gives the grace it signifies.

Catholics believe that in the sacraments Christ himself acts, and that they are effective by his action, provided that they are celebrated validly and received with the right disposition. Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist are the sacraments of initiation. The sacraments are also understood as the ordinary ways in which believers receive the grace of salvation. A Protestant reader should note that most Protestant churches recognize only two, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, and that the Catholic list includes rites that Protestants regard as not instituted by Christ in the same way.
lds.sacraments:
Latter-day Saints use the word ordinances for the sacred rites of their faith, and they teach that certain ordinances are essential for exaltation, and are called saving ordinances. They are baptism, confirmation and the gift of the Holy Ghost, priesthood ordination for men, and for those who are able, the temple endowment and the sealing of marriage.

The sacrament, meaning the weekly bread and water in remembrance of Christ, is also an ordinance, as are blessings for the sick and naming of children. Each ordinance must be performed by someone with proper priesthood authority, and each involves covenants with God. Ordinances may also be performed by proxy for the dead. A Protestant reader who thinks of two ordinances should note that Latter-day Saints have more, and that they attach great importance to the authority to perform them.
ortho.sacraments:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of the Holy Mysteries, rather than of sacraments, a Greek word that stresses that God acts in ways that are beyond full understanding. The Orthodox generally list seven, which are Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist, Confession, Ordination, Marriage and Holy Unction, but they do not draw a rigid boundary around the number.

The Orthodox understand the Mysteries as ways in which God gives his grace through material things such as water, oil, bread and wine, and as part of the whole life of the church, which is itself a Mystery. They are not seen as separate acts by which grace is dispensed, but as ways of participating in Christ. A Protestant reader accustomed to two ordinances or sacraments should note that the Orthodox include more, and understand them as belonging together in the church's life.
catholic.sacred_music:
The Catholic Church has a long tradition of sacred music in worship, including Gregorian chant, the sung prayer of the Western church, choral polyphony and music for the organ. The Second Vatican Council taught that Gregorian chant should be given pride of place in liturgical services, and that the treasury of sacred music should be preserved.

Since the Council, the Mass is usually celebrated in the local language, and hymns in the local language are common, sometimes with guitars and other instruments, and practice varies widely from one parish to another. The Church teaches that music in worship should be beautiful and prayerful, and should serve the liturgy. A Protestant reader accustomed to congregational hymns or worship bands should note that Catholic worship values chant and choral music, and that much of the Mass itself is sung.
evangelical.sacred_music:
Many Evangelical churches use contemporary worship: a worship band with guitars, drums and keyboards leads the congregation in modern songs, with the words often projected on screens. Songs are frequently sung in a longer set, with the congregation standing and, in some churches, raising their hands.

Others continue to use traditional hymns, sung with an organ or piano, and many churches combine both. Disagreements over style have sometimes been called the worship wars. Evangelicals generally understand music as a way of praising God, and of expressing faith and emotion, and many see it as a major part of the service. A Protestant reader from a church with a set liturgy and hymnal should note that Evangelical worship is often built around a flexible program with a music set and a sermon.
ortho.sacred_music:
Eastern Orthodox worship is sung almost entirely, and the music is chant. There are several traditions, including Byzantine chant in Greek churches and znamenny chant in Russian ones, alongside choral arrangements in four parts, especially in Slavic churches. Music is normally unaccompanied by instruments.

The texts of the hymns are the main focus, and the music is understood as serving them, since the hymns carry much of the church's teaching about feasts and saints. Byzantine tradition uses a system of eight tones, which set the melodies for each week. The Orthodox regard the music as part of the church's tradition, and not as a place for individual performance. A Protestant reader accustomed to congregational hymns or a worship band should note that in Orthodoxy a choir or chanter leads and the people join in.
catholic.salvation:
Catholics teach that salvation is God's gift of friendship and eternal life, made possible through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is received through faith, Baptism and the life of the Church, and is meant to be worked out over a lifetime. Catholics often say that they have been saved, are being saved, and hope to be saved.

The Church teaches that God wills all people to be saved, and that salvation involves being justified, made holy, and finally glorified in heaven. Faith is understood as working through love, and grace is given through the sacraments. Catholics do not generally claim a certainty of final salvation, but a confident hope. A Protestant reader who speaks of being saved as a settled matter should note that Catholic teaching treats salvation as a process and as a relationship that is to be kept and deepened.
evangelical.salvation:
Evangelicals speak of being saved: rescued by God from sin and its consequences, through faith in Jesus Christ, who died in the place of sinners and rose again. They understand salvation as a gift of grace, received by faith and not by works, in line with the words of the Letter to the Ephesians.

Many Evangelicals describe a moment of conversion when a person repents and trusts in Christ, and are able to say that they are saved. They also speak of salvation as continuing, in being saved from the power of sin in daily life, and as finally completed in heaven. Assurance is often stressed. A Protestant reader from a liturgical or sacramental tradition should note that Evangelicals stress a personal decision of faith, and use the language of being saved as a normal way to speak about a believer's standing before God.
lds.salvation:
Latter-day Saints use the word salvation in more than one sense. In the broadest sense it means being saved from physical and spiritual death, through Jesus Christ's atonement. Everyone will be resurrected as a free gift of grace, and nearly everyone will inherit some degree of glory.

They also speak of exaltation, or eternal life, which is the fullest salvation, living in God's presence as families and becoming like him. It requires faith in Christ, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, temple covenants and enduring to the end. Latter-day Saints stress that all of this depends on Christ's grace, and that no one can save himself. A Protestant reader who uses salvation to mean forgiveness of sins and eternal life with God should note that Latter-day Saints distinguish between salvation in general and exaltation in particular.
ortho.salvation:
The Eastern Orthodox Church understands salvation as healing and union with God, which it often calls theosis, meaning becoming partakers of the divine nature. It is a gift of God's grace made possible by Christ's death and resurrection, and it begins in Baptism and continues throughout a person's life.

The Orthodox usually speak of being saved, as a continuing process, and not simply of having been saved at a moment. Salvation involves the person's cooperation with grace through prayer, repentance, the sacraments and love of neighbor. Sin is understood as sickness and bondage to death, and Christ as the physician and victor over death. A Protestant reader who uses the word saved to speak of a completed status should note that the Orthodox emphasize a journey of transformation, though they too say that salvation is entirely God's gift.
catholic.sanctification:
Catholics teach that God calls every Christian to holiness, and that sanctification is the process by which grace makes a person holy and more like Christ. It begins with Baptism, in which sanctifying grace is given, and grows through the sacraments, prayer, the practice of virtue and works of charity.

The Second Vatican Council taught that all the faithful, in any state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of love. Sanctification is understood as God's work, in which the person cooperates, and it may continue after death, in purgatory. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics do not sharply separate sanctification from justification, and that they see growth in holiness as belonging to the same process of receiving God's grace.
holiness.sanctification:
Holiness churches teach entire sanctification, sometimes called Christian perfection: that God's grace can free a believer, in this life, from the power of sin and fill the heart with perfect love. It is understood as a gift received by faith, not as a level reached by human effort.

This does not mean the believer is beyond weakness or mistakes. Holiness teachers distinguish sin, meaning a willful turning from God, from the human limitations and errors that remain. A sanctified person can still grow, and can still fall if faith and obedience are neglected. A Protestant reader from a Reformed or Lutheran background, which teaches that believers remain sinners throughout life, should note that Holiness churches teach that a decisive cleansing is possible in this life.
lds.sanctification:
Latter-day Saints teach that sanctification is the process of becoming holy, and of being cleansed from sin by the power of Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost. It is a change of nature, through which a person becomes more like Christ, and ultimately worthy to live in God's presence.

They connect it with baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, the sacrament and temple covenants, and with the person's own obedience and repentance. A sanctified person is described in scripture as one who has yielded his heart to God. Latter-day Saints stress that it is possible only through the grace of Christ, and that it takes place over a lifetime. A Protestant reader will find the idea of being made holy familiar, and should note the connection with ordinances and covenants.
methodist.sanctification:
Methodists follow John Wesley in teaching that the Christian life is meant to grow in holiness, a journey which Wesley called going on to perfection. Christian perfection means perfect love: loving God with all the heart and loving one's neighbor as oneself. It is not a claim to be free of mistakes, weakness or ignorance, and it is a gift of God's grace received by faith, not an achievement.

Methodists differ in how they understand this. Some, especially in Wesleyan and Holiness bodies, expect a definite moment of entire sanctification, while others emphasize gradual growth throughout life. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, which teaches that sanctification is progressive but never complete in this life, should note that Methodists hold that real transformation is possible, and that believers should expect it and pray for it.
ortho.sanctification:
The Eastern Orthodox Church understands sanctification as part of the whole process of salvation, in which the Holy Spirit makes a person holy by sharing in God's own holiness. It is not separated from justification, and is closely connected with theosis, the growth into union with God.

Sanctification begins with Baptism and Chrismation, and continues through the sacraments, prayer, fasting, repentance and works of love. It involves the struggle to overcome the passions. The saints are those who have been most fully sanctified. A Protestant reader who distinguishes justification from sanctification should note that the Orthodox see them as aspects of one continuing work of God, and speak of holiness as sharing in God's life rather than as reaching a moral standard.
catholic.schism:
In Catholic teaching, schism is the refusal of submission to the pope, or of communion with the members of the Church who are subject to him. It is understood as a grave sin against the unity of the Church, distinct from heresy, which is the denial of a truth of the faith.

The Catholic Church has regarded the separation of the Eastern Orthodox churches, which is dated to 1054, as a schism, and the Reformation as involving both heresy and schism. Today the Church speaks more gently of the separated churches, and acknowledges that those born into them are not personally guilty of the sin of separation. A Protestant reader who uses the word division should note that Catholics use schism in a technical sense, connected to the authority of the pope, and that they see it as something to be healed through dialogue and prayer.
ortho.schism:
In Eastern Orthodox teaching, schism means a break in communion within the Church, and the Orthodox regard it as a serious wound to the unity that Christ willed. The break between the churches of the East and the West, usually dated to 1054, is understood by the Orthodox as the result of departures by the Western church, such as the claims of the pope to universal authority and the addition of the filioque to the Creed.

Schisms have also occurred within Orthodoxy, such as that of the Old Believers in Russia in the seventeenth century, and there are disputes over which churches are canonical, that is, in proper communion. The Orthodox hold that schism is healed by a return to unity in faith and sacraments, and not by compromise. A Protestant reader who uses the word division for the many separations of the Reformation should note that the Orthodox use schism for a break in communion, and see it as calling for repentance.
catholic.scripture:
Catholics call the Bible Sacred Scripture and revere it as the word of God written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. The Catholic Bible contains seventy-three books, including the deuterocanonical books that Protestant Bibles omit or print separately. Scripture is read at every Mass, and the Church has always used it in prayer and teaching.

Catholics teach that Scripture and Tradition together form the one sacred deposit of the word of God, entrusted to the Church, and that the Church's teaching office interprets it. The Second Vatican Council urged that access to Scripture should be widely available and encouraged Catholics to read it. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics revere the Bible as God's word, as Protestants do, and differ in the books included and in the belief that Scripture is not to be read apart from the Church.
christian_science.scripture:
Christian Scientists regard the Bible and Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, by Mary Baker Eddy, as their pastor together. The Bible is the record of God's revelation, and Science and Health is understood to explain its spiritual meaning in a way that can be tested and proved in daily life.

In Christian Science churches there are no ordained clergy. Sunday services consist of readings from the Bible and from Science and Health, arranged in a weekly Bible Lesson which is studied by members during the week. A Protestant reader who treats the Bible alone as the word of God should note that Christian Scientists honor the Bible, and treat the second book as an authoritative interpretation of it, which is not accepted as Scripture by other churches.
lds.scripture:
Latter-day Saints have four books of scripture, called the standard works: the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. In English they generally use the King James Version of the Bible. They regard the Book of Mormon as another testament of Jesus Christ, and the others as modern revelation.

They hold the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly, and they read all four books together, studying them in a yearly course in Sunday School and at home. Words of living prophets, when given by the Holy Ghost, are also considered scripture. A Protestant reader who takes the Bible as the only scripture should note that Latter-day Saints honor the Bible, but read it alongside three more books which they believe to be inspired.
ortho.scripture:
The Eastern Orthodox Church honors the Holy Scripture, the Bible, as the inspired word of God, and as the church's own book. Its Old Testament follows the Greek Septuagint, which includes books that Protestants call the Apocrypha, and its New Testament is the same as in other churches.

Scripture is at the center of Orthodox worship. The Gospel book is enthroned on the altar, and is carried in procession and read aloud in every Divine Liturgy, and the services are full of the words of the Psalms and other biblical texts. The Orthodox hold that Scripture is to be understood within the Church, in the light of Holy Tradition and the Fathers. A Protestant reader should note that Orthodox Christians revere the Bible, and read it as part of the life of the church and not as an independent authority.
adventist.second_coming:
Adventists place the Second Coming of Christ at the center of their hope, and the word Advent in their name means coming. They teach that Jesus will return personally, visibly and audibly, in glory, and that his coming will be world-wide and unmistakable, as described in the Gospel of Matthew.

At his coming the righteous dead will be raised and the righteous living will be taken to be with him, and the wicked will be destroyed. Adventists teach that his return is near, as shown by the signs of the times. The movement arose after a failed expectation of Christ's return in 1844, and Adventists since have not set dates, holding to the words of Jesus that no one knows the day or the hour. A Protestant reader should note that Adventists do not teach a secret rapture, but a single, open return.
catholic.second_coming:
Catholics confess that Christ will come again in glory, an event they call the Parousia, to judge the living and the dead, and to bring history to its fulfillment. The Church teaches that the time is unknown, and that believers should live in readiness for it. It also teaches that before the return there will be a final trial for the Church, involving a great deception.

The expectation is expressed in the liturgy: at each Mass the people proclaim that Christ has died, Christ is risen, Christ will come again, and the season of Advent prepares for both his first coming at Christmas and his final coming. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and Protestants share the belief in a personal, visible return, and should note that Catholics do not teach a rapture separate from it, and do not make speculation about its timing a matter of doctrine.
lds.second_coming:
Latter-day Saints teach that Jesus Christ will come again to the earth, personally and in glory, as taught in the Bible and in their own scriptures. Its time is not known, but it will be preceded by signs, including the restoration of the gospel and its preaching in all the world.

At his coming, the righteous will be caught up to meet him, and the wicked will be destroyed, and the earth will be cleansed. It will begin the thousand years of peace called the Millennium, in which Christ will reign. Latter-day Saints stress preparing for the Second Coming by living the gospel, and the church's prophets and apostles speak of it as a reason for faithfulness. A Protestant reader will find the hope in Christ's return familiar, and should note that Latter-day Saints connect it with the Restoration and with temple work.
ortho.second_coming:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, as the Nicene Creed says, and that his kingdom will have no end. The Second Coming is called the Parousia, and it will bring the general resurrection, the judgment and the renewal of all creation.

Orthodox worship keeps this hope before the faithful. In Holy Week, the hymn of the Bridegroom, who comes at midnight, calls believers to be watchful, and the church's prayers ask for a good defense at the Last Judgment. The Orthodox do not speculate about the timing or sequence of the end times, and do not teach a rapture separate from Christ's coming. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox share the expectation of Christ's visible return, and stress readiness of heart rather than prediction.
catholic.separated_brethren:
Catholics have used the phrase separated brethren to refer to other baptized Christians who are not in full communion with the Catholic Church. The phrase was common at the time of the Second Vatican Council. Its idea is that those who are baptized and believe in Christ are truly brothers and sisters, though divided from the Catholic Church.

In recent years, the Church has more often used phrases such as other Christians, separated brothers and sisters, or Christians of other churches and ecclesial communities. Catholics believe that these communities preserve many elements of the faith, and that the Holy Spirit works through them. A Protestant reader should note that the term was meant as a warm one, and reflects the Catholic teaching that baptism creates a real bond among Christians, though some now find it patronizing and prefer other terms.
evangelical.separated_brethren:
Evangelicals often distinguish between nominal Christians, people who are counted as Christians by name or by church membership but who do not have a personal faith in Christ, and true believers, who have been born again. They use the term other believers for Christians in other churches whom they regard as genuinely converted.

This means that Evangelicals do not generally divide people by denomination. They recognize believers in many churches, and also believe that some members of their own churches may be nominal. The language can sound judgmental to those who hear it, since it implies that a person's membership in a church is not enough. A Protestant reader should note that Evangelicals see the phrase as expressing concern for a living faith, and not as a comment on any church's teaching, though how they view Catholic and Orthodox Christians varies among them.
ortho.separated_brethren:
Eastern Orthodox Christians commonly use the terms heterodox and non-Orthodox to refer to Christians outside the Orthodox Church. Heterodox means holding other teaching, and it is a descriptive term, meaning that a person or church differs from Orthodox teaching, and is not necessarily an accusation of heresy.

Some Orthodox use harsher language for groups they regard as departing from the faith, and others prefer to speak simply of non-Orthodox Christians and to avoid labels. Orthodox teaching generally holds that the Orthodox Church is the Church, while leaving the standing of other Christians to God. A Protestant reader who is described as heterodox should note that the word is an old technical one, and that its use reflects the Orthodox belief that unity requires common faith, not that the person is considered outside God's mercy.
catholic.sexual_ethics:
Catholics teach that sexuality is a good gift from God, and that it is to be lived with the virtue of chastity, which means the integration of one's sexual desires in a way that is appropriate to one's state of life. Chastity applies to everyone: to the married, who are to be faithful, and to the unmarried and those in celibate vocations, who are to abstain.

The Church holds that sexual union is proper only within marriage between a man and a woman, and that it should be both unitive and open to life. On this basis it teaches that sex outside marriage, contraception, pornography and homosexual acts are contrary to God's design, while insisting that all persons must be treated with respect and compassion. A Protestant reader should note that the Catholic teaching rests on an understanding of natural law, as well as on Scripture, and that it is presented as a call to love and holiness.
evangelical.sexual_ethics:
Most Evangelicals teach what they call biblical sexual ethics: that sexual intimacy is a gift from God to be enjoyed within marriage between one man and one woman, and that sex outside marriage, adultery, pornography and same-sex sexual relationships are contrary to God's design. They base this on passages from Genesis, the teaching of Jesus about marriage and the letters of Paul.

Evangelicals stress that all people are sinners in need of grace, and that forgiveness and restoration are available in Christ. Many churches have tried to emphasize purity and chastity, especially for young people. Churches differ in their tone, and a minority of Evangelicals hold different views on same-sex relationships. A Protestant reader from a tradition that has changed its teaching on some of these matters should note that Evangelicals generally hold that Scripture speaks clearly on the subject.
lds.sexual_ethics:
Latter-day Saints follow the law of chastity: sexual relations are to be reserved for a man and a woman who are legally and lawfully married, and are to be avoided outside marriage. Members are also asked to be completely faithful to their spouses, and to avoid pornography and immodesty.

The church teaches that sexual intimacy in marriage is sacred and good, and that it is part of God's plan for creating families. Same-sex attraction is understood as not itself a sin, while acting on it is contrary to the law of chastity, and members are taught to treat everyone with love and respect. Those who break the law are called to repent, with the help of Church leaders. A Protestant reader from a conservative tradition will find much that is familiar, and should note that the standards are tied to temple worship and eternal marriage.
ortho.sexual_ethics:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that sexual union belongs within marriage between a man and a woman, and that chastity means faithfulness in marriage and abstinence outside it. Marriage is a mystery, in which the couple's love is blessed by God, and sexuality is a good part of it.

The Orthodox tradition also honors celibacy, especially in monastic life, as a path of self-offering to God. Sexual sin, like other sin, is understood as a sickness of the soul that calls for repentance, confession and healing, and the church's approach is generally pastoral, with the guidance of a spiritual father. A Protestant reader should note that Orthodox teaching is similar in its basic rules to that of other historic churches, and that it stresses ascetic discipline, fasting and prayer as means of keeping chastity.
anglican.sign_of_the_cross:
In Anglican churches the sign of the cross is used in baptism, when the newly baptized person is signed with the cross as a mark of belonging to Christ, and by many worshippers at the blessing, the creed and other points in the service. It is a way of confessing faith in the Trinity and in the cross of Christ.

Its use is a matter of custom and freedom. Anglo-Catholics and many others make the sign of the cross frequently, and many Evangelical Anglicans do not. The Book of Common Prayer's baptismal service includes the signing with the cross, and no Anglican church forbids the practice. A Protestant reader from a church where the gesture is not used should note that Anglicans regard it as a gesture of devotion, and not as having power in itself.
catholic.sign_of_the_cross:
Catholics make the sign of the cross by touching the forehead, the chest, and the left and right shoulders with the right hand, while saying: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. It is a short prayer which confesses faith in the Trinity and in Christ's death on the cross.

Catholics make it at the beginning and end of prayers, at the start of Mass, on entering a church and touching holy water, and at blessings, and many make it in daily life, for example before meals. It is a reminder of Baptism, which was given in the name of the Trinity. A Protestant reader for whom the gesture is unfamiliar should note that Catholics do not believe it has magical power, and see it as a physical way of praying and of committing oneself to Christ.
lutheran.sign_of_the_cross:
Lutherans use the sign of the cross as a reminder of Baptism and of Christ's cross. Luther's Small Catechism directs that it be made in the morning and evening prayers, and it is commonly used in the liturgy at the invocation of the Trinity, at the blessing and at the absolution, and in the baptism service.

It is not commanded by Scripture and is not required, so its use is a matter of Christian freedom, and some Lutherans use it often while others seldom. It is understood as a confession of faith and of trust in Christ, and as a way to remember that one belongs to him. A Protestant reader from a tradition that avoids the gesture should note that Lutherans do not treat it as having power in itself, and stress that it points to Christ and his promise.
oriental_ortho.sign_of_the_cross:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, use the sign of the cross frequently in worship and in daily life. It is made with the right hand, and expresses faith in the Trinity and in the cross of Christ, and it is made at the start of prayers, at the entrance to a church, at blessings and at many points in the liturgy.

The exact way of making it, including how the fingers are held and which direction the hand moves, differs among these churches, and each has its own tradition, going back many centuries. Icons and crosses are also honored. A Protestant reader for whom the gesture is unfamiliar should note that in these churches it is a normal expression of prayer, and that it is an outward sign of faith in the Trinity and the cross, and not a rite that has power in itself.
ortho.sign_of_the_cross:
Eastern Orthodox Christians make the sign of the cross with the right hand, joining the thumb and the first two fingers together to represent the Trinity, and folding the other two fingers into the palm, to represent the two natures of Christ, divine and human. They touch the forehead, the chest, and then the right shoulder and the left shoulder, which is the opposite order from Catholic practice.

The sign is made very frequently: at the beginning and end of prayers, at mention of the Trinity, when entering or leaving a church, when passing an icon, and many times during the Divine Liturgy. It is a way of praying with the whole body, and confessing the cross. A Protestant reader for whom the gesture is unfamiliar should note that for the Orthodox it is a normal part of prayer, and is not thought to have power in itself.
anglican.sola_scriptura:
Anglicans hold that Holy Scripture contains all things necessary for salvation, and that nothing which is not read in it or proved by it may be required as an article of faith. This is stated in the Thirty-Nine Articles. Scripture is therefore the primary and decisive authority in the church.

Anglicans do not, however, set Scripture against the church's tradition. They read the Bible in the light of the ancient creeds and the teaching of the early church, and they use reason to understand and apply it. This is often summarized as Scripture, tradition and reason, and is associated with the teacher Richard Hooker. A Protestant reader who holds to Scripture alone should note that Anglicans agree that Scripture has the final word, and use tradition and reason as aids in understanding it.
catholic.sola_scriptura:
Catholics do not teach that Scripture is the only authority for Christian faith. They hold that Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from the same divine source, and together form the one sacred deposit of the word of God, which is entrusted to the Church. Tradition means the teaching of the apostles handed down in the Church, and not later human customs.

The Church's teaching office, the Magisterium, is understood to interpret both, and to serve them. Catholics point out that the Church determined which books belong to the Bible, and that the Bible does not itself say that it is the sole authority. A Protestant reader who holds to sola scriptura, Scripture alone, should note that Catholics revere Scripture as the highest written authority, and differ in believing that it should be read within the living Tradition of the Church.
lutheran.sola_scriptura:
Lutherans hold that Scripture alone is the norm for teaching and life in the church: it is the source and standard by which all doctrine is judged. The Lutheran Confessions, gathered in the Book of Concord, are honored as a faithful exposition of what Scripture teaches, but they are subject to Scripture and not above it.

This does not mean that Lutherans reject the church's earlier tradition. They keep the ancient creeds, the church's liturgy and much of its worship, and they value the teachers of the early church. What they insist is that tradition serves Scripture and can be corrected by it. A Protestant reader from a Baptist or Evangelical background should note that Lutherans hold to Scripture alone, and also value the confessions and the liturgy as guides, in a way that gives tradition a more prominent place in their churches.
ortho.sola_scriptura:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not accept the principle of Scripture alone. It teaches that Scripture must be understood together with Holy Tradition, meaning the whole life of the Church guided by the Holy Spirit, which includes the creeds, the decisions of the ecumenical councils, the writings of the Fathers, the liturgy and the icons.

The Orthodox do not treat Scripture and Tradition as two separate sources. Scripture is the highest written expression of the church's faith, and Tradition is the living context in which it was written and is rightly understood. They point out that the church existed before the New Testament was written. A Protestant reader who holds to sola scriptura should note that the Orthodox honor the Bible highly, and consider that separating it from the church that produced it leads to different interpretations.
reformed.sola_scriptura:
Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final authority in matters of faith and life. The Westminster Confession states that the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in Scripture, or may by good and necessary consequence be deduced from it, and that nothing is to be added to it.

Reformed churches value confessions and catechisms, such as the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Standards, which summarize what Scripture teaches, and they honor the teaching of the early church. Yet these are subordinate standards which are tested by Scripture, and can be corrected by it. The Holy Spirit is understood to persuade believers of the truth and authority of Scripture through the Word itself. A Protestant reader will find this the familiar Protestant principle, held by Reformed churches with particular attention to confessions as summaries of the Bible's teaching.
adventist.soul_sleep:
Adventists teach that human beings do not have an immortal soul that lives apart from the body. They understand the soul to be the whole person, as in the account in Genesis that man became a living soul when God breathed life into the body, and they hold that at death the person ceases to be conscious until the resurrection.

This is often called soul sleep, though Adventists more commonly speak of the state of the dead. They cite the passage in Ecclesiastes that the dead know nothing, and Jesus' description of the death of Lazarus as sleep. They find comfort in the hope of resurrection at Christ's return. A Protestant reader who believes that believers are conscious with the Lord after death should note that Adventists read the same passages differently, and think that the idea of an immortal soul came into Christianity from Greek philosophy.
catholic.soul_sleep:
Catholics teach that every human being has a spiritual and immortal soul, created directly by God at the moment of conception. At death the soul is separated from the body, and is judged by Christ. It does not sleep or cease to exist, but goes to heaven, purgatory or hell, and awaits the resurrection of the body at the end of time.

The Church rejects the idea that the soul is extinguished at death or that it is unconscious. Its teaching about the immortal soul is connected with the belief in the particular judgment, prayers for the dead and the communion of saints, since those who have died are still alive in Christ. A Protestant reader who is used to the view that the dead are conscious with the Lord will find much in common with Catholic teaching, though not with groups such as Adventists that teach soul sleep.
christadelphian.soul_sleep:
Christadelphians speak of the sleep of the dead. They teach that human beings do not have an immortal soul that lives on after death. At death a person is entirely dead, unconscious, and waits in the grave until the resurrection.

The hope is therefore resurrection and judgment when Christ returns, and not a heaven or hell immediately after dying. Those judged faithful are raised to eternal life in the kingdom of God on a renewed earth, and the rest do not live again to suffer forever. Christadelphians support this from Scripture passages which liken death to sleep. A Protestant reader who believes that the dead are conscious with the Lord should note that Christadelphians read the same passages as describing an unconscious state until the resurrection.
jehovahs_witnesses.soul_sleep:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the soul is the person, and not a separate immortal part which lives on after the body dies. When a person dies, he or she ceases to exist, and the dead are unconscious, as a passage in Ecclesiastes describes, with no knowledge of anything.

The hope for the dead is therefore the resurrection: God will remember them and bring them back to life. Witnesses find comfort in this, and see it as more realistic than an idea that the dead are already in heaven. They do not believe that the dead can hear the living, or that the living can communicate with them. A Protestant reader who believes that the soul survives death should note that Witnesses hold that the Bible presents death as a sleep from which God will awaken people.
seventh_day_adventist.soul_sleep:
Seventh-day Adventists teach that death is an unconscious state, and that human beings have no immortal soul apart from the body. They hold that the whole person, body and spirit, is a unity, and that at death the person rests until the resurrection, at Christ's second coming, when the righteous are raised to immortality.

This belief is part of the church's official statement of beliefs. It is linked with their caution about spiritualism, meaning attempts to communicate with the dead, which they regard as deceptive, since the dead are not conscious. A Protestant reader who believes that Christians at death go to be with the Lord should note that Adventists regard that belief as depending on the idea of an immortal soul, which they do not accept, and see the resurrection as the true hope.
lds.spirit_world:
Latter-day Saints teach that when a person dies, the spirit leaves the body and goes to the spirit world, where it lives until the resurrection. The spirit world has two parts: spirit paradise, a state of peace and rest for the righteous, and spirit prison, for those who did not accept the gospel or who lived wickedly.

It is a place of activity and learning, not of sleep.
