They teach that righteous spirits preach the gospel to those in spirit prison, who can accept it and repent, and that living members perform baptisms and other ordinances for them in temples. A Protestant reader who knows the words Hades and Sheol as the realm of the dead should note that Latter-day Saints understand the spirit world as a time of continued opportunity, not of final judgment.
catholic.sunday_worship:
Catholics are obliged to attend Mass on Sundays and on certain holy days, unless prevented by a serious reason such as illness. Sunday is the Lord's Day, the weekly celebration of Christ's resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week, and the Church teaches that missing Mass without a serious reason is a grave matter.

Catholics are also asked to rest from unnecessary work on Sundays, so that they can worship, spend time with family and enjoy leisure. A Mass on Saturday evening, called the Vigil Mass, satisfies the obligation. Many Protestants also keep Sunday as the day of worship, but do not usually treat attendance as an obligation binding in conscience. A Protestant reader should note that for Catholics Sunday Mass is regarded as the center of the week, and is a duty as well as a privilege.
ortho.sunday_worship:
The Eastern Orthodox Church keeps Sunday as the Lord's Day, the weekly celebration of the Resurrection, which the Orthodox sometimes call a little Pascha. The main worship is the Divine Liturgy on Sunday morning, and in many parishes there is also a service of Vespers on Saturday evening, which prepares for Sunday.

Orthodox Christians are expected to attend the Divine Liturgy each Sunday, and to receive communion regularly with preparation. Sunday is a day of joy, and fasting is set aside in most cases. The church does not lay down strict rules about rest, as in some Protestant traditions, and the emphasis is on worship. A Protestant reader who treats Sunday as a day of rest and worship will find that the Orthodox regard it as the day when the community gathers around the Eucharist to celebrate Christ's victory over death.
catholic.temples:
Catholics do not use the word temple for their church buildings in the way some other traditions do. A Catholic church is a house of God and of prayer, in which the Mass is celebrated and the Blessed Sacrament is reserved in a tabernacle. A church is solemnly dedicated, and is treated with reverence, and is open to all who wish to pray.

The Catholic Church also teaches that the baptized are living temples of the Holy Spirit, following the language of the First Letter to the Corinthians, and that the Church as a whole is the temple of God. There are no secret rites which only certain members may attend in Catholic church buildings. A Protestant reader who thinks of the body of the believer as a temple will find that Catholics agree, and should note that Catholics also regard a church building as a sacred place because of the presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
community_of_christ.temples:
Community of Christ has a Temple in Independence, Missouri, dedicated in 1994. It is understood as a place of worship, prayer, education and reconciliation, dedicated to the pursuit of peace, and it is generally open to visitors and to people of every faith or none.

This differs from the temples of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, where rites such as the endowment and sealings are performed and access is limited. Community of Christ does not practice those ordinances. The Temple's daily prayer for peace and its ministries of healing and study express the church's emphasis on peace, justice and the worth of all persons. A Protestant reader who knows the word temple from the Bible should note that Community of Christ uses it for a house of prayer and peace, open to the public.
lds.temples:
Latter-day Saints build temples as houses of the Lord, and distinguish them from their ordinary meetinghouses, where Sunday worship takes place. Temples are places for sacred ordinances such as the endowment, marriage sealings for time and eternity, and baptisms and other ordinances performed on behalf of the dead.

Only members in good standing who hold a temple recommend may enter a temple once it has been dedicated, though the public is invited to tour it before dedication. Members wear special clothing in the temple, and the ceremonies are held private, which is a matter of sacredness and not of secrecy. A Protestant reader who thinks of the temple of the Bible as no longer needed, or as the body of the believer, should note that Latter-day Saints believe that temples have been restored, and treat them as central to their worship.
